but it's something that I thought you might find a little bit interesting and help you get a little bit of a better handle on the relationship between an image and a container.
When we were going over the flow of actions that occurred while we were building the image, we spoke about how we'd take an image from the previous step,
we created a container out of it, we'd do something with that container, and we then essentially create an image out of that running container,
or that kind of very temporarily, temporary container that was created.
So at this point, you and I know very well that we use images to create containers,
but based on everything that we've been talking about in this section, it sure seems like the opposite is kind of true as well.
It seems like we can kind of take a container and generate an image out of it as well,
and that actually is correct.
You and I can manually create a container, run some commands inside of it, or change its file system,
and then generate a usable image that we can then use at some point in the future.
In other words, we can kind of very manually do the same thing that our Docker file does.
We can create a container, run a command, like say APK at Redis right here, and then generate an image out of that.
I want to very quickly show you how that would look, but again, I really don't expect you to do this on your own personal project.
I'm just showing this as kind of something you might find interesting.

we're then going to install Redis on it, we're then going to set up a default command,

so that we can run a couple of commands inside of it.
So I'm going to put on the IT flag, I'll put on alpine as our image,
and then the command that I want to execute inside there is SH to start up a shell.
So then I get presented with a command prompt right here that is inside of that running container.
And so inside that container, I'm going to manually install Redis by running APK add dash dash update Redis like so.
So we now have a running container where we have modified its file system,
and the file system has now seen the installation of Redis.
So we've got the running container, I'm now going to open up a second terminal window,
and inside of here, I'm going to run a command using the Docker CLI
that's going to essentially take a snapshot of that running container and assign a default command to it
and generate an image out of the entire thing.
So to do so, I'll say first Docker PS to get the idea that running container,
and then we'll do Docker commit.
I'm going to add on a dash C right here, which is going to allow us to specify the default command.
So I'm going to say dash C, and then I'll put an CMD.
Double quotes inside the square brace, Redis dash server,
I'll close the double quote, I'll close the square brace,
and I'll close the single quote.
So notice how we have a single quote single quote and double quotes around it.
And then after all that, I'll paste the idea of that running container.
So I'm going to paste it in like so.
And the output is the idea of a new image that we just customized for our own uses.
Now you'll notice how this is a really long idea right here.
One shortcut that I haven't quite mentioned so far.
Whenever you're making use of IDs or hashes in the Docker world,
you don't have to copy the entire thing.
You can just copy a segment of the start,
and it's kind of assumed that this is going to be unique enough.
The Docker is going to take this and realize that,
oh, you're probably talking about this very long idea right here.
So I'm going to copy just an arbitrary number of leading characters here,
and then we'll do a Docker run that,
and that's going to start up a new container out of the image that we just created.
And inside that running container,
we already have Redis installed,
and the default starting command will be to run Redis server.
So let's run that,
and we'll very quickly see all the typical output that we see from a running Redis instance.
All right, so like I said,
we basically just very manually created a container,
added a dependency to the container,
set up the default command, and then generated an image out of all that.
Again, you really don't want to use that practice in general.
You don't use Docker commit in general.
You really want to use the Docker file approach,
because it allows you to very easily rerun that series of steps again in the future.
But again, I just like you might find interesting how,
yes, there really is a very kind of fluid relationship
between containers and images.
